content.value:
In a raw OpMode, everything lives inside loop(). Driving code, arm control, sensor checks, and button handling all get mixed together.

A single 200-line loop() is hard to read and harder to debug.

A Command is a single action wrapped in a class.

It knows when to start, what to do each tick, and when it's finished.

Commands are reusable across different OpModes and can be chained together to build complex sequences.

A Subsystem represents one piece of hardware: the drivetrain, an arm, or a claw.

Each subsystem owns its motors and sensors.

Commands use subsystems through clean public methods like drive(), stop(), or raise().

Only one command can use a subsystem at a time.

The CommandScheduler runs in a loop, calling execute() on every active command each tick.

It checks isFinished() to know when commands are done, calls end() for cleanup, and enforces the rule that only one command can use each subsystem. Basically, it is the brain of the command-based system.

FTC teams use command-based because it scales.

Adding a new arm subsystem doesn't touch existing drive code.

Autonomous routines are built from small, tested building blocks.

TeleOp and auto share the same commands.
